claims.text: The proposed starting material is a coarse-grained, single-phase Cantor-type CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has an intact passive oxide film after standard processing.
The controlled comparison exposes one sample to sliding in 3.5 wt% NaCl and keeps an otherwise identical sample stationary.
High-strain-rate sliding produces severe near-surface grain refinement.
High-strain-rate sliding dynamically amorphizes the near-surface region.
The resulting ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous-like layer has increased hardness.
The transformed near-surface layer lowers friction.
Increased hardness and lower friction enhance wear resistance.
Fine-grained near-surface microstructure weakens the passive layer.
Wear-induced nanostructural transformation disrupts the continuity and protective quality of the passive oxide film.
Weakening the passive film reduces the corrosion resistance of the Cantor alloy.
A compromised passive film in chloride solution accelerates localized corrosion.
The coupled degradation response is governed by a trade-off between improved wear resistance and accelerated corrosion.
The sliding sample will have a lower wear rate than the unworn stationary baseline.
The sliding sample will have a higher localized corrosion rate than the stationary baseline.
Over extended exposure, total degradation may be similar to or greater than that of the stationary baseline because corrosion offsets reduced mechanical wear.
The prediction applies when contact severity is sufficient to induce the proposed nanostructural transformation and chloride attacks the compromised passive film.
The prediction should fail when sliding does not generate the nanocrystalline or amorphous layer.
The prediction should fail in inert environments where corrosion is negligible.
Absence of significant grain refinement or amorphization, or absence of an increased corrosion rate in worn samples, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a lower wear rate for the sliding sample relative to an unworn stationary sample. A stationary sample has no imposed sliding wear, so its wear rate is zero or undefined; it is not a valid matched baseline for claiming reduced wear rate.
